analysis.one_liner: Blocks a Labor Department rule that narrowed which companies owe workers minimum wage and overtime.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the House Education and Labor Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: In January 2020 the Labor Department issued a rule narrowing when two companies count as a worker's joint employer under the nation's wage-and-hour law. Before the rule, a brand like a fast-food chain or a lead contractor could be on the hook if its franchisee or subcontractor shorted workers on minimum wage or overtime; the rule limits that liability mainly to companies that directly control the worker. This bill would bar the Labor Department from putting that rule into effect, keeping the broader standard that lets workers collect from the bigger company at the top of the chain.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers hired through subcontractors, temporary agencies, and franchises. If a lead company shares responsibility for an employer's wage violations, workers have a second, better-funded company to recover unpaid wages and overtime from — an important backstop when the direct employer is thinly capitalized and cannot pay.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit the Labor Department from implementing or enforcing the January 16, 2020 final rule on joint employer status under the Fair Labor Standards Act.

The bill's findings state that under the broader economic-realities standard, workers in subcontracted and franchised workplaces could hold the top company jointly liable for minimum wage, overtime, and child labor violations, and that the new rule rejects that standard in favor of a narrower control-based test.
The bill's findings cite an Economic Policy Institute estimate that the rule could increase wage theft and workplace fissuring enough to cost workers more than a billion dollars a year.

analysis.who_pays: Franchisors, lead contractors, and staffing or temp agencies that would once again face joint liability for wage-law violations at the firms they hire through. They would bear greater exposure to back-pay claims and compliance costs, some of which could be passed to consumers or small franchisees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Franchisors, lead contractors, and staffing agencies

drawbacks.text: Businesses argued the 2020 rule gave companies clearer, more predictable standards for when they are legally responsible for workers hired through franchisees and contractors, replacing what they saw as an uncertain test. Restoring broader liability increases legal risk and compliance costs for franchisors and lead firms.

The bill is a one-topic response that would block a single regulation by statute; it does not set a joint-employment standard itself, so the underlying question of when two companies share liability for a worker would remain unsettled after the rule was blocked.
Broader joint liability can raise costs for the outsourced firms that specialize in these work arrangements, and lead companies might respond by changing or reducing the work they contract out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers the bill covers, the benefit is direct: a better-funded company at the top of the chain can be made to pay wages that a thinly capitalized direct employer cannot, which the bill's own findings say could be worth over a billion dollars a year in recovered wages. The cost falls on franchisors, lead contractors, and staffing agencies in the form of joint liability and compliance costs, some of which may reach consumers. The main weakness of the bill itself is that it is a narrow veto of one rule rather than a legislative standard for joint employment.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Joseph Kennedy III introduced the bill on March 12, 2020, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
No other member cosponsored the bill.
The committee never held a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill targeted the Labor Department's January 16, 2020 final rule on joint employer status, which narrowed the standard for when two companies share liability for wage and hour violations.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Franchisors, lead contractors, and staffing and temp agencies came out ahead: the narrower joint-employer rule stayed in effect, keeping liability for wage violations concentrated with direct employers and shielding top-of-chain companies from back-pay claims. Workers in subcontracted and franchised jobs did not gain the second company to collect from.

for.name: Joseph P. Kennedy III
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and stated in its findings that the Labor Department rule would increase wage theft by letting companies outsource liability to thinly capitalized intermediaries.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Department of Labor
against.role: Labor Department under the Trump administration
against.what_they_did: Published the January 16, 2020 joint employer rule that the bill sought to block, narrowing the standard for shared wage-law liability.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the only recorded support was its Democratic sponsor; the partisan shape of the wider chamber was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would block the rule that narrowed their exposure to joint liability for wage-law violations by franchisees and subcontractors, restoring a broader standard under which workers could collect unpaid wages from the top company. Their interest in keeping the rule runs against workers seeking back pay.

industries.industry: Staffing and temp agencies and labor intermediaries
industries.note: These firms operate as the direct employer in outsourced work arrangements; the bill would keep the broader standard under which the companies hiring them can share liability, which the bill's findings say discourages using thinly capitalized intermediaries to avoid wage obligations.

industries.industry: Workers in subcontracted and franchised jobs
industries.note: The bill would keep the broader joint-employment standard, giving these workers a better-funded company to recover minimum wage and overtime from when a direct employer cannot pay.
